text: Which tissue most often preserves endogenous ancient DNA in temperate burials?
choices: Petrous portion of the temporal bone

text: Why is the petrous bone valuable for paleogenomics?
choices: Its dense structure can shelter DNA

choices: DNA copied from a reference genome

text: Why are short DNA fragments typical in ancient samples?

text: Why are ancient DNA libraries often built from single-stranded molecules?
choices: They can recover highly fragmented molecules

text: What does uracil-DNA glycosylase treatment partially reduce?

choices: Damage signal decreases while authenticity evidence weakens
Contamination rises while DNA length increases
Capture specificity falls while coverage doubles
Sex inference disappears while barcodes improve

text: What does PCR duplication usually indicate in a low-input library?
choices: Repeated sequencing of the same original molecules

text: Which library feature helps identify samples after pooling?
What is index hopping in multiplex sequencing?
choices: Misassignment of reads to another library
Movement of an individual between populations
Loss of Y chromosomes during burial

text: Why are terminal C-to-T substitutions informative?
choices: They can reflect cytosine deamination near fragment ends
They prove a sample is from Europe
They show every read is unique

text: Which pattern supports authentic ancient DNA rather than modern contamination?
choices: Only reads matching the lab worker

text: What does mapDamage estimate from aligned ancient reads?
choices: Fragment length and nucleotide misincorporation patterns

text: Why can mitochondrial DNA be easier to recover than nuclear DNA?
What does a mitochondrial haplogroup primarily trace?
What does the Y chromosome chiefly inform in ancient population studies?
Why is sex estimation from ancient DNA sometimes uncertain?
choices: Low coverage can obscure sex-chromosome balance
Y markers occur equally in all genomes

text: What does an X-to-autosome coverage ratio help estimate?
Why are transition substitutions modeled in ancient DNA analyses?
choices: They are enriched by deamination damage

text: What is a molecular consensus sequence intended to represent?
choices: The inferred original sequence across observations
The longest read in a library

text: How can paired-end sequencing help ancient DNA analysis?
choices: It records both ends and improves fragment placement
It doubles the number of chromosomes

text: What is shotgun sequencing in paleogenomics?
choices: Sequencing a broad mixture of library molecules
Reading collagen peptides instead of DNA

text: What is hybridization capture designed to enrich?
Why can mitochondrial capture be useful?
choices: It raises coverage for maternal-line analysis

text: What is in-solution capture generally more efficient than?
What does genomic coverage describe?
choices: The average number of reads per reference position

text: Why does low coverage complicate diploid genotype calling?
choices: Alleles may be missed by sparse observations
Reads become too long to align

text: What is pseudo-haploid calling commonly used for?
choices: Sampling one observed allele at each covered site

text: Which statistic is often used to test allele sharing among populations?
In an f4 statistic, what does a value near zero commonly suggest?
choices: No detectable asymmetry in the tested allele sharing
Complete identity of all four populations

text: What does an f3 admixture statistic test in a basic framework?
choices: Whether a target may be admixed between two sources

text: What is a qpAdm model attempting to estimate?
choices: Mixture proportions for a target from candidate sources
The number of PCR cycles used
The age of each sequencing read

text: Why are outgroups included in formal population tests?
What does genetic drift most directly change between populations?
choices: Allele frequencies through sampling and reproduction

text: What does effective population size represent?
choices: A genetic measure of reproductive contribution
The census count of excavated individuals
The number of reads in a BAM file
The volume of extracted bone powder

text: What does a bottleneck leave in population genomic data?
choices: Uniform damage at every fragment end

text: Why can principal components be misleading for ancient samples?
choices: Missing data and projection choices affect positions
Damage is always removed before PCA
Every axis has a biological interpretation

text: What is a common purpose of ADMIXTURE-like clustering?
choices: Summarizing ancestry components under a chosen model

text: Why should ancestry components not be treated as literal ancient tribes?
choices: They are statistical summaries dependent on references and K
They are direct observations of social identity
They exclude all modern genetic variation

text: What is linkage disequilibrium decay useful for estimating?
Why can recent admixture produce long ancestry tracts?
choices: There has been less recombination since mixing

text: What does chromopainter-style analysis model?
choices: Chromosome segments as copied from reference donors

text: What is IBD sharing evidence of?
choices: Long inherited segments from a common ancestor

text: Why is contamination estimation especially important for mitochondrial genomes?
choices: A minor contaminant can distort high-copy haplotypes

text: What does schmutzi estimate in ancient mitochondrial analysis?
Why can related individuals bias population analyses?
choices: They overweight a single family’s ancestry
They increase the number of outgroups
They convert diploid calls to haploid calls

text: What is pseudo-replication in an archaeological dataset?
choices: Treating related or repeated samples as independent evidence

text: Why can kinship analysis be valuable before population modeling?
choices: It identifies close relatives and reduces sampling bias
It determines the exact migration route

text: What does phasing assign across a chromosome?
Why is phasing difficult with low-coverage ancient genomes?
choices: Few molecules span multiple heterozygous sites

text: What does imputation infer in a sparse ancient genome?
choices: The exact age of each fragment

text: Why must imputation references be chosen cautiously?
choices: Poorly matched references can bias inferred ancestry
Reference panels prevent every genotype error
Modern panels contain no population structure

text: What is a principal ethical concern in destructive ancient DNA sampling?
choices: Removing irreplaceable material from human remains
Increasing the number of sequencing reads

text: Why should descendant communities be consulted in paleogenomic research?
choices: They may hold rights, interests, and cultural knowledge
They determine every base call computationally
They eliminate the need for laboratory controls
They guarantee a preferred population model

text: What does a responsible data-access plan balance?
choices: Scientific reuse with privacy, consent, and community concerns
Sequencing speed with read length only

text: Which evidence most strongly supports a claimed population replacement?
choices: Concordant genetic, archaeological, and chronological evidence

text: Why can cultural change occur without large-scale genetic replacement?
choices: Ideas and technologies can spread between populations

text: What does a ghost population in a mixture model denote?
choices: An unsampled ancestral lineage inferred indirectly

text: Why is source selection critical in qpAdm analyses?
choices: Poor sources can make proportions or fit misleading
Any source set gives identical estimates
Outgroups are unnecessary with many sources

text: What can a cline of ancestry proportions indicate?
choices: Gradual gene flow or geographic structure

text: Why can time-stratified sampling clarify demographic history?

It replaces the need for radiocarbon dates

text: What does an allele-frequency spectrum summarize?
choices: Counts of variants by their observed frequencies
The lengths of every DNA fragment

text: Why can selection complicate neutral demographic inference?
choices: Selected loci may not follow drift-only expectations
Selection removes all ancient DNA damage
Neutral loci always have no mutations

text: What is ascertainment bias in SNP panels?
choices: Variants are discovered unevenly in particular populations
All populations receive equal marker representation
Damage is amplified at every SNP
Reads are assigned to the wrong sample by design

text: Why are transition-rich SNP panels potentially risky for ancient DNA?
choices: Damage can mimic alleles at affected sites
Transitions never occur in modern genomes

text: What is transversion-only analysis sometimes used to reduce?
Why can radiocarbon dates and genetic estimates disagree?
choices: They measure different processes and carry distinct uncertainties
Genetic data contain no temporal information
Both methods always estimate the same event

text: What is a temporal sampling bias in paleogenomics?
choices: Overrepresenting some periods relative to others
Including both sexes in a dataset

text: Why should negative controls be sequenced when feasible?
choices: They reveal contaminant sequences introduced during processing
They provide the target’s missing chromosomes

text: What does a position-dependent damage model estimate?
choices: The probability that each burial layer contains a different population
Misincorporation probabilities as a function of fragment distance from an end
The number of alleles expected after every PCR cycle
The fraction of reads assigned to each mitochondrial haplogroup

text: Why can terminal damage correction alter genotype likelihoods?
choices: It converts a diploid genotype into a phased haplotype
It removes reference bias from every capture experiment
It changes the error probabilities assigned to observations near fragment ends
It replaces a population allele frequency with a read count

text: What is the main rationale for partial rather than complete UDG treatment?
choices: Preserving all endogenous molecules while removing every contaminant
Increasing fragment length by repairing both DNA strands
Enabling direct phasing of chromosomes from single molecules
Retaining a small terminal damage signal while reducing internal uracils

text: How can mitochondrial contamination be estimated without a known contaminant haplotype?
choices: By counting only reads carrying terminal cytosine substitutions
By comparing read likelihoods under endogenous and alternative mitochondrial sequences
By treating every heteroplasmic site as a contaminant allele
By inferring contamination from the specimen’s radiocarbon measurement

text: Why can hybridization capture distort population comparisons?
choices: Capture always removes all damaged molecules from every population equally
Target enrichment converts allele frequencies into unbiased genotype calls
Probe mismatches can make sequence recovery depend on ancestry or divergence
Probe pools prevent microbial DNA from entering the extraction

text: What does a genotype-likelihood framework retain that hard calls discard?
choices: The exact chromosome phase of every low-coverage heterozygote
A guarantee that every observed base is endogenous
The complete sequencing history of each molecular duplicate
Uncertainty among possible genotypes given reads, errors, and allele frequencies

text: Why are genotype likelihoods preferable to consensus calls at very low coverage?
choices: They infer missing alleles without using any reference frequencies
They make postmortem substitutions biologically informative by definition
They ensure each individual contributes exactly two observations per site
They propagate read-level uncertainty into downstream population statistics

text: What does a significantly nonzero D-statistic generally indicate?
choices: That all four populations descend from one recent individual
Unequal allele sharing inconsistent with the tested simple tree
That sequencing depth is identical across the four populations
That the outgroup must be the direct ancestor of the target

text: Under what condition can D-statistics be difficult to interpret?
choices: Unequal relatedness, gene flow, or an unsuitable outgroup violates the simple comparison
Any positive value proves a single documented migration event
The statistic is unaffected by ascertainment or missing data
A significant Z-score means every tested SNP is independently informative

text: What key assumption underlies a basic qpAdm mixture interpretation?
choices: Candidate sources span the target’s ancestry relative to informative outgroups
Each source population is genetically homogeneous through all periods
The target must be an exact first-generation child of the sources
All outgroups are equally close to every candidate source

text: Why can adding a source improve qpAdm fit without proving its historical role?
choices: Correlated sources can absorb residual structure without uniquely identifying ancestry
Every added source is automatically dated to the target’s context
A better p-value establishes that the source directly migrated into the target
qpAdm estimates are independent of source covariance and outgroup choice

text: What does a sequentially Markov coalescent model approximate?
choices: The genealogy along a genome while simplifying correlations among neighboring loci
The chemical conversion of cytosine into uracil after burial
The movement of captured molecules between probe and wash solutions
The probability that a read belongs to a modern contaminant

text: Why can ancient genomes challenge coalescent demographic inference?
choices: Sparse data, temporal structure, and damage can confound estimated population histories
Coalescent models require mitochondrial DNA from every excavated individual
Ancient samples contain no information about allele-frequency change
Demographic models assume that all archaeological samples are unrelated by definition

text: What evidence most directly supports a first-degree genetic relationship?
choices: Excess allele sharing and a kinship coefficient consistent with parent-offspring or siblings
Matching mitochondrial haplogroups without any autosomal comparison
Similar radiocarbon dates and burial orientation
The same principal-component position after projection

text: Why can full siblings be harder to distinguish from second-degree relatives?
choices: Their expected autosomal sharing distributions overlap in finite, noisy data
Siblings always share identical mitochondrial genomes with all second-degree relatives
Second-degree relatives cannot share long IBD segments
Kinship estimates ignore missingness and sequencing error by construction

text: Which result is strongest for authenticating an ancient human genome?
choices: Human mapping, damage patterns, fragment profiles, and contamination estimates agree
A high read count from one library without extraction blanks
A close match to a modern reference individual alone
A population assignment that fits the archaeological interpretation

text: Why is damage alone insufficient to authenticate endogenous ancient DNA?
choices: Modern molecules can acquire damaged bases, and contaminants may also show terminal errors
Damage patterns identify the exact excavated individual without comparison
Only endogenous molecules can contain cytosine deamination
Authenticity requires no assessment of mapping quality or contamination
